<!-- Home.md -->

# compost

compost deploys docker-compose applications to your own servers. A server gets shared services that many apps use: a **Caddy** reverse proxy with automatic HTTPS, **Postgres** databases, a **Keycloak** login provider and **OpenObserve** for logs, metrics and traces. Each app is linked to them by a few lines of YAML next to its compose file.

compost is a single CLI on your machine. It reaches servers over SSH, or manages this machine directly. It installs no agent: a server only holds plain files in one folder and Docker containers.

```sh
compost server deploy --apply                              # Caddy + Postgres on the server
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-staging.yaml   # your app, with a database and a domain
```

## What it does for you

- **Routing and HTTPS:** domains and paths go to your services through Caddy, with certificates from Let's Encrypt.
- **Databases:** each app gets its own Postgres database and user, and its services get the connection variables.
- **Logins:** an app can get a Keycloak realm, client and test users, with the OIDC settings passed to its services.
- **Monitoring:** the output and metrics of apps and shared services go to OpenObserve, and services get the variables to send OpenTelemetry traces.
- **Instances:** the same app runs as `staging`, `prod` or a review copy, each with its own domains and data.
- **Secrets:** passwords live in files you don't commit, or are stored on the server; generated ones are kept between deploys.
- **Backup and restore:** apps and shared services, to this machine or to a folder on the server, also to make copies or move to a new server.
- **Gradual migration:** Caddy serves existing containers, apps link to existing or hosted databases (e.g. AWS RDS), and `compost.yaml` can live apart from apps you don't own. See [Migrating to compost](Migration.md).

Your compose file is never changed. compost adds networks and variables in an override file on the server.

## Concepts

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Server** | A host compost manages, reached over `ssh` or `local` (this machine). It has a name in your local config. |
| **Context** | The default server for commands, set with `compost connect <server>`. |
| **Shared app** | A server-wide service built from a built-in type: `caddy` (kind `ingress`), `postgres` (kind `database`), `keycloak` (kind `oidc`), `openobserve` (kind `monitoring`). Defined in `compost-server.yaml`. |
| **App** | Your application: a compose file plus `compost.yaml`. |
| **Instance** | One deployment of an app on a server, `<app>-<prefix>`, e.g. `myapp-staging`. |
| **Overlay** | A YAML file with the values of one instance (prefix, domains, passwords), merged over `compost.yaml`. |
| **Link** | A connection between an instance and a shared app: a domain on the ingress, a database, a login realm, log collection. |
| **Manager key** | A UUID that marks which compost installation manages a server. Copy it to manage the same servers from another machine. |

## Requirements

| Side | Needs |
|---|---|
| Your machine | Linux or macOS, the `compost` binary, an OpenSSH client |
| Server | Linux, POSIX `sh` and `tar` (BusyBox is enough), Docker Engine 24 or newer with the compose v2 plugin |
| Server user | Logs in with an SSH key, member of the `docker` group (no sudo) |

<!-- Installation.md -->

# Installation

compost is a single binary with no dependencies. Linux builds are static and run on any distribution. On your machine it needs `ssh`; servers need Docker with compose v2 (see [Home](Home.md#requirements)).

## With the install script

The script detects your system, downloads the latest release, verifies its checksum and installs to `~/.local/bin`:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost/raw/branch/master/scripts/install.sh | sh
```

Options go after `sh -s --`:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--version vX.Y.Z` | Install this release instead of the latest |
| `--to <dir>` | Install into this directory instead of `~/.local/bin` |

```sh
curl -fsSL https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost/raw/branch/master/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- --version vX.Y.Z --to /usr/local/bin
```

## By hand

Download the archive for your system and `SHA256SUMS` from the [releases page](https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost/releases):

| System | Archive |
|---|---|
| Linux x86_64 | `compost-vX.Y.Z-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` |
| Linux arm64 | `compost-vX.Y.Z-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` |

```sh
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf compost-vX.Y.Z-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz
install -m 755 compost-vX.Y.Z-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/compost ~/.local/bin/compost
compost --version
```

Each release also has the documentation for AI agents: `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` and `compost-skill-vX.Y.Z.tar.gz` (see [AI agents](AI-Agents.md#from-a-release)).

## macOS

There are no prebuilt macOS binaries yet. Build from source with [Rust](https://rustup.rs):

```sh
cargo install --locked --git https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost --tag vX.Y.Z
```

## Set up

```sh
compost init
```

This creates `~/.compost` with a new manager key (see [Files and folders](Files-and-Folders.md#on-your-machine)). Every other command except `server generate`, `app generate` and `agent` needs it.

To manage servers that another machine already manages, use its key:

```sh
compost init --key 0d6c2f5e-7c55-4c1e-9a5b-3f1f1f0e2a11
```

The key is in `~/.compost/compost-manager.yaml` on the other machine. A server managed by a different key shows as `FOREIGN` and compost refuses to change it.

## Update and uninstall

To update, install again. Your configuration in `~/.compost` stays.

To uninstall, delete the binary and `~/.compost`. Servers keep running; their files are in `~/.compost-server` of the server user.

Next: [Quick start](Quick-Start.md).

---

<!-- Quick-Start.md -->

# Quick start

Run compost against this machine with the sample app from the repository: a web page and a Python API with a Postgres database, behind Caddy. You need Docker with compose v2. It uses port 18080 and plain HTTP, so it runs next to anything already on ports 80 and 443.

```sh
git clone https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost.git
cd compost/samples
```

## 1. Define this machine as a server

```sh
compost init
compost server define dev --local     # compost's folder here: ~/.compost-server
compost connect dev                   # the default server from now on
compost server state                  # dev (local): UNINITIALIZED
```

## 2. Start the shared apps

```sh
cd server
compost server deploy --apply -f compost-server.yaml,compost-server.local.yaml
```

`compost-server.yaml` defines Caddy, Postgres 18, Keycloak and OpenObserve for a real server. `compost-server.local.yaml` is an overlay that changes Caddy to port 18080 without TLS, Keycloak to `http://auth.localhost:18080` and OpenObserve to `http://logs.localhost:18080`. Files given with `-f` are merged in order; see [Configuration](Configuration.md#how-files-are-merged).

compost generates the passwords it needs. Keycloak takes a minute or two to start the first time.

```sh
compost server state
# dev (local): OK
#   Docker …, home /home/you/.compost-server
#   ingress    caddy-main       caddy 2  running
#   database   postgres18       postgres 18  running
#   monitoring monitoring       openobserve 1  running
#   oidc       keycloak         keycloak 26  running
```

## 3. Deploy the app

```sh
cd ../sampleapp
cp .compost-local.example.yaml .compost-local.yaml
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-local.yaml
```

compost uploads the folder, builds the images, creates a database and user for the app, passes `DATABASE_URL` to the services that need it, sends their output to OpenObserve, runs the migration and routes `sampleapp.localhost` through Caddy.

```sh
curl -H 'Host: sampleapp.localhost' http://localhost:18080/api/hits   # {"hits": 1, "mode": "local"}
```

Browsers resolve `*.localhost` to this machine, so you can also open http://sampleapp.localhost:18080/.

## 4. Look around

```sh
compost app list                      # instances on the server
compost app state sampleapp-local     # services, domains, database
compost connector list                # shared apps and what is linked to them
```

## 5. Clean up

```sh
compost app remove sampleapp-local --purge database --yes
```

`--purge database` also drops the app's database; without it the data stays for the next deploy. The shared apps keep running. To stop them:

```sh
docker compose -p compost-ingress-caddy-main down
docker compose -p compost-database-postgres18 down
docker compose -p compost-oidc-keycloak down
docker compose -p compost-monitoring-monitoring down
```

Their files are in `~/.compost-server/shared/`.

## Next

- See the sample's logs and metrics: [Examples](Examples.md#logs-and-metrics-in-openobserve).
- Add a Keycloak login to the sample: [Examples](Examples.md#log-in-with-keycloak).
- Set up your own app: [Applications](Applications.md).
- Deploy to a real server: [Production setup](Production-Setup.md).

<!-- Production-Setup.md -->

# Production setup

From an empty Linux server to your app on HTTPS. Shared apps are configured in an infrastructure folder (e.g. a Git repository), and each app in its own repository.

## 1. Prepare the server

- Linux with Docker Engine 24 or newer and the compose v2 plugin.
- A user (by default `compostuser`) in the `docker` group, who can log in with your SSH key. compost needs no root.
- Ports 80 and 443 open, and your domains' DNS records pointing to the server, so Caddy can get certificates from Let's Encrypt.

Connect once by hand, so SSH asks you to accept the host key. compost never turns off host key checking.

```sh
ssh compostuser@203.0.113.10
```

## 2. Define it

```sh
compost init                                     # once per machine
compost server define prod --address 203.0.113.10
compost connect prod
compost server state                             # prod (…): UNINITIALIZED
```

`server define` takes `--user`, `--port`, `--identity-file` and `--server-home` (see [Servers and shared apps](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#defining-servers)). It only writes your local config, nothing on the server.

Every command that talks to a server picks it in this order: `-s <name>` → the `COMPOST_SERVER` variable → the context set by `connect`.

## 3. Shared apps

In your infrastructure folder:

```sh
compost server generate --with caddy,postgres    # or without --with to pick from a list
```

This writes:

| File | Content | Commit? |
|---|---|---|
| `compost-server.yaml` | The shared apps, set up for this machine (Caddy on port 18080, no TLS) | yes |
| `compost-server.prod.yaml` | What a real server changes: ports 80/443, [`tls: auto`](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#tls), `acme_email` | yes |
| `.compost-server.secrets.example.yaml` | The secret keys with placeholders | yes, as an example |

Set `acme_email` in `compost-server.prod.yaml`. Then copy the secrets example and set real passwords, or remove keys you want compost to generate:

```sh
cp .compost-server.secrets.example.yaml .compost-server.secrets.yaml   # never commit this one
compost server deploy --apply -f compost-server.yaml,compost-server.prod.yaml,.compost-server.secrets.yaml
compost server state
```

Generated passwords are kept on the server and reused. The Postgres `root_password` and Keycloak `admin_password` can't change after the first deploy.

## 4. Your app

In the app's repository, next to `docker-compose.yaml`:

```sh
compost app generate                             # compost.yaml + .compost.secrets.example.yaml
```

Edit `compost.yaml`: uncomment the ingress routes and database links you need (see [Applications](Applications.md)). Then give each instance its values. You can keep them in a local file:

```sh
cp .compost.secrets.example.yaml .compost-staging.yaml        # prefix, domains, passwords
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-staging.yaml
```

or store them on the server, so any machine (and CI) deploys with `compost.yaml` alone:

```sh
compost secret deploy .compost-staging.yaml --prefix staging
compost app deploy --apply --prefix staging
```

See [Secrets](Secrets.md). Files named `.compost-*.yaml` and `.compost.*.yaml` are never uploaded with the sources.

## 5. Day to day

```sh
compost app deploy --apply --prefix staging      # deploy a new version: same command
compost app deploy --dry-run --prefix staging    # what would change, without changing anything
compost app list
compost app state myapp-staging
compost connector list
```

To skip `--apply` on every deploy:

```sh
compost config set deploy.apply true             # all servers
compost config set deploy.apply false --for-server prod   # but not this one
```

Without `--apply` (and with `deploy.apply` off), deploys only upload and render files; nothing is restarted.

## 6. Backups

Set where backups go in `compost-server.yaml` and deploy it:

```yaml
backup:
  target: server       # archives stay on the server, in ~/.compost-server/backups
```

Then, e.g. from cron on your machine:

```sh
compost app backup --all
compost server backup
```

See [Backup and restore](Backup-and-Restore.md), also for moving to a new server.

## Checklist

- [ ] DNS for every domain points to the server before the first deploy with `tls: auto` (see [TLS](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#tls)).
- [ ] `.compost-server.secrets.yaml` and `.compost-<env>.yaml` are in `.gitignore`.
- [ ] `~/.compost/compost-manager.yaml` is backed up: without the key you can't manage the server (or use `init --key` with the value from the server's `~/.compost-server/manager_key`).
- [ ] Backups run and you have tried a restore.

<!-- Examples.md -->

# Examples

The repository's [`samples/`](https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost/src/branch/master/samples) folder has a server setup (Caddy, Postgres, Keycloak) and an app (web page, Python API, migration). [Quick start](Quick-Start.md) deploys them on this machine.

## Static site

```yaml
# docker-compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .             # e.g. FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine, listens on 8080
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
name: mysite
deployment:
  build: true
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      routes:
        - {name: main, target: web, port: 8080}
app_services:
  - {name: web, service: web}
```

```yaml
# .compost-prod.yaml
prefix: prod
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      domains: [example.com, www.example.com]
```

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

## API with a database and a migration

From [`samples/sampleapp`](https://gitrepo.dev.org.pl/dev.org.pl/compost/src/branch/master/samples/sampleapp). The migration runs once before the backend starts; compose's `depends_on` handles the order and compost counts an exit with code 0 as healthy.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yaml
services:
  web:
    build: ./web
    restart: unless-stopped
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes: [visits:/data]
    depends_on:
      migrate: {condition: service_completed_successfully}
  migrate:
    build: ./backend
    command: ["python", "migrate.py"]
volumes:
  visits:
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
name: sampleapp
deployment:
  build: true
services:
  database:
    - name: main-db
      type: postgres
      version: ">=16"
      targets: [backend, migrate]
      environment:
        DATABASE_URL: db_url
  ingress:
    - name: site
      routes:
        - {name: api, target: backend, port: 5000, path: /api}
        - {name: web, target: web, port: 8080}
app_services:
  - {name: web, service: web}
  - {name: backend, service: backend, environment: {APP_MODE: production}}
  - {name: migrate, service: migrate}
backup:
  volumes: [visits]
```

```yaml
# .compost-staging.yaml
prefix: staging
services:
  database:
    - name: main-db
      db_name: sampleapp_staging
      db_user: sampleapp
      db_password: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
  ingress:
    - name: site
      domains: [staging.example.com, www.staging.example.com]
app_services:
  - name: backend
    environment:
      APP_MODE: staging
```

## Staging and production from one repository

Each overlay is an instance. They share `compost.yaml` and the server's shared apps, with separate domains, databases and containers.

```sh
compost secret deploy .compost-staging.yaml
compost secret deploy .compost-prod.yaml
compost app deploy --apply --prefix staging
compost app deploy --apply --prefix prod
compost app list
```

Or on two servers: `-s staging-server` and `-s prod-server`.

## An app you don't own, from a deployment repository

Deploy a third-party app pinned to a release, without adding files to its repository:

```
deploy/
├── wiki/
│   ├── compost.yaml
│   ├── compose.prod.yaml
│   └── .compost-prod.yaml       not committed
└── upstream/wiki/               git submodule, checked out at a release tag
```

```yaml
# deploy/wiki/compost.yaml
name: wiki
deployment:
  source_dir: ../upstream/wiki
  compose_overrides: [compose.prod.yaml]
services:
  database:
    - name: main
      type: postgres
      version: ">=16"
      targets: [app]
      environment:
        DB_URL: db_url
  ingress:
    - name: site
      routes:
        - {name: web, target: app, port: 3000}
app_services:
  - {name: app, service: app}
```

```yaml
# deploy/wiki/compose.prod.yaml: the upstream file brings its own database; compost's is used instead
services:
  db: {profiles: [off]}
  app:
    depends_on: !reset {}
    deploy:
      resources: {limits: {memory: 1g}}
```

```sh
cd deploy/wiki
git -C ../upstream/wiki checkout v2.5.0
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

## An app on AWS RDS

The database is hosted; compost creates the app's database and user there with the RDS master user, and backs it up like its own:

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: rds-main
      type: postgres
      version: 16
      external:
        host: main.abc123.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com
        sslmode: require
      configuration:
        root_user: postgres            # the master user; root_password in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
services:
  database:
    - name: main
      type: postgres
      instance: rds-main               # external databases are always pinned
      targets: [backend]
      environment:
        DATABASE_URL: db_url           # …?sslmode=require
```

The server must reach RDS (security group, VPC). `compost server state` shows `external, accepting connections` when it does.

## Log in with Keycloak

With Keycloak in `compost-server.yaml` (see [Servers and shared apps](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#keycloak-oidc)), add an OIDC link to the sample app:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
services:
  oidc:
    - name: login
      type: keycloak
      targets: [backend]
      environment:
        OIDC_ISSUER: oidc_issuer
        OIDC_INTERNAL_URL: oidc_internal_url
        OIDC_CLIENT_ID: oidc_client_id
        OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET: oidc_client_secret
```

Per instance, give the realm its own domain and a test user:

```yaml
# .compost-local.yaml
services:
  oidc:
    - name: login
      realm: sampleapp
      public_url: http://login.localhost:18080
      redirect_uris: ["http://sampleapp.localhost:18080/*"]
      users:
        - {username: alice, email: alice@example.com, first_name: Alice, last_name: Doe, password: alice-password}
  ingress:
    - name: login
      domains: [login.localhost]
      routes:
        - {name: realm, link: oidc/login}
```

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-local.yaml
curl -H 'Host: login.localhost' http://localhost:18080/realms/sampleapp/.well-known/openid-configuration
# {"issuer":"http://login.localhost:18080/realms/sampleapp", ...}
```

`alice` can log in at http://login.localhost:18080/realms/sampleapp/account/. The Keycloak admin console is at the provider's own URL (http://auth.localhost:18080/admin/), as `admin` with the password from `~/.compost-server/shared/oidc/keycloak/secrets/keycloak.env`.

To remove the login, delete both entries and deploy with `--purge oidc`; without it the realm, client and users stay in Keycloak.

## Logs and metrics in OpenObserve

Add a monitoring app to `compost-server.yaml`, and let Caddy and Postgres send their output to it. Caddy serves OpenObserve's UI and also sends its own access log there:

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      configuration:
        access_log: true
      monitoring: {}            # output, and Caddy's metrics
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
      monitoring: {}
  monitoring:
    - name: monitoring
      type: openobserve
      version: 1
      configuration:
        url: http://logs.localhost:18080
```

```sh
compost server deploy --apply
grep root_ ~/.compost-server/connectors/monitoring/monitoring/root-connector.yaml   # login for the UI
```

Then link the app. `optional: true` keeps the app deployable on servers without monitoring:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
services:
  monitoring:
    - name: telemetry
      optional: true
      targets: [web, backend, migrate]
      metrics:
        - {target: backend, port: 5000, path: /metrics}   # if the backend serves Prometheus metrics
      environment:                     # for an OpenTelemetry SDK in the backend
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: otlp_endpoint
        OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: service_name
        OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: resource_attributes
```

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-local.yaml
compost connector list
# monitoring
# └─ monitoring  openobserve 1  running
#    ├─ sampleapp-local/telemetry  logs web, backend, migrate; metrics sampleapp-local-backend:5000/metrics  app: deployed
#    ├─ shared database/postgres18/monitoring  logs postgres
#    └─ shared ingress/caddy-main/monitoring  logs caddy; metrics compost-ingress-caddy-main-caddy:9180/metrics
```

Open http://logs.localhost:18080/ and log in. The `docker` log stream holds the output of all of them; filter with `fluent_tag = 'sampleapp-local.backend'`. Metrics have a stream each, such as `caddy_http_requests_total` and `container_memory_usage_total`; traces from the SDK show under Traces.

## A review copy of production

```sh
compost app backup myapp-prod -o prod.compost.tar.gz
compost app restore prod.compost.tar.gz --prefix review -f review-domains.yaml
# … test …
compost app remove myapp-review --purge database --volumes --yes
```

`review-domains.yaml` gives the copy its own domains. Its database is a new one named after the `review` prefix, filled from production's dump.

## Nightly backups

```sh
# crontab on your machine
30 2 * * *  compost -s prod app backup --all --target server
45 2 * * *  compost -s prod server backup --target server
```

`compost -s prod backup list` shows what's there.

## An app with its own database

An app whose compose file runs its own MariaDB has no `database` link for compost to dump, and copying its data folder while it runs isn't safe. Dump it into a volume before each backup, and load it after a restore:

```yaml
# compose file
services:
  db:
    image: mariadb:11
    environment: {MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: …}
    volumes: [db-data:/var/lib/mysql, db-dumps:/dumps]
    healthcheck:                  # `after_restore` waits until it accepts connections
      test: [CMD, healthcheck.sh, --connect, --innodb_initialized]
volumes: {db-data: {}, db-dumps: {}}
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [db-dumps]
  before_backup:
    - exec: db
      command: mariadb-dump -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --all-databases --single-transaction > /dumps/all.sql
  after_restore:
    - exec: db
      command: mariadb -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" < /dumps/all.sql
```

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml    # stores the steps
compost app backup myapp-prod
compost app restore myapp-prod-….compost.tar.gz --include volumes --replace --yes
```

The restore stops the app, puts the dump back into `db-dumps`, starts it and loads the dump. More in [Backup and restore](Backup-and-Restore.md#steps-around-a-backup-or-restore).

---

<!-- Migration.md -->

# Migrating to compost

How to move a server that runs Docker containers set up by hand (a reverse proxy, apps, their databases) to compost, one step at a time. Every phase ends with everything working, and every step can be undone.

| Phase | What changes | Downtime |
|---|---|---|
| [1. The proxy](#phase-1-caddy-replaces-the-proxy) | compost's Caddy serves your existing sites | seconds |
| [2. Shared services](#phase-2-shared-services) | compost's Postgres (and Keycloak) run next to the old ones; old databases are registered as external | none |
| [3. Apps, one by one](#phase-3-apps-one-by-one) | compost deploys the app; it keeps its database and volumes | while the app starts |
| [4. Data, when convenient](#phase-4-data-into-compost) | the app's data moves into compost's Postgres and volumes | a short stop of that app |
| [5. Clean up](#phase-5-clean-up) | old containers, networks and volumes go | none |

compost only adds its own folder (`~/.compost-server`) and containers whose names start with `compost-` or with your apps' instance names. It never touches containers it did not create.

## Before you start

Take stock of what runs:

```sh
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Ports}}'
docker network ls
docker volume ls
docker compose ls                     # compose projects and their folders
```

Note for each app: its compose project and file, its domains, its database (container, name, user, password), and its named volumes. Find the proxy configuration (nginx `server` blocks, Traefik labels, Caddyfile).

Back up every database and volume the usual way before you change anything.

Then set up compost on your machine and define the server ([Production setup](Production-Setup.md#2-define-it)):

```sh
compost init
compost server define prod --address 203.0.113.10
compost connect prod
compost server state                  # prod (…): UNINITIALIZED
```

The SSH user must be in the `docker` group. compost can then see and join the existing containers' networks.

## Phase 1: Caddy replaces the proxy

compost's Caddy can join the Docker networks of your existing containers (`networks`) and serve sites you write yourself (`sites`), so it takes over the proxy's job as it is.

```sh
compost server generate --with caddy  # in your infrastructure folder
```

Translate each site of the old proxy into an entry of `sites`. `config` is the inside of a Caddyfile site block:

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      version: 2
      configuration:
        http_port: 80
        https_port: 443
        tls: auto
        acme_email: admin@example.com
        # Existing networks of the containers the sites proxy to.
        networks: [shop_default, blog_default]
        sites:
          - name: shop
            domains: [shop.example.com, www.shop.example.com]
            config: |
              reverse_proxy backend:5000
          - name: blog
            domains: [blog.example.com]
            config: |
              encode gzip
              reverse_proxy blog-ghost-1:2368
```

Upstreams are reached on the joined networks by compose service name (`backend`) or container name (`blog-ghost-1`).

<details>
<summary>Translating common nginx and Traefik setups</summary>

| nginx | Caddy `config` |
|---|---|
| `location / { proxy_pass http://backend:5000; }` | `reverse_proxy backend:5000` |
| `location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api:8080/; }` | `handle_path /api/* {`<br>`  reverse_proxy api:8080`<br>`}` |
| `client_max_body_size 50m;` | `request_body {`<br>`  max_size 50MB`<br>`}` |
| `return 301 https://example.com$request_uri;` (other domain) | a separate site: `redir https://example.com{uri} permanent` |
| `ssl_certificate …` | nothing: Caddy gets certificates itself |

Traefik labels such as ``traefik.http.routers.shop.rule=Host(`shop.example.com`)`` with `traefik.http.services.shop.loadbalancer.server.port=5000` become a site with `domains: [shop.example.com]` and `reverse_proxy <service>:5000`.

</details>

Check, switch, check:

```sh
compost server deploy --dry-run       # validates; lists the networks it joins
docker stop old-proxy                 # or: docker compose -p proxy stop
compost server deploy --apply
curl -I https://shop.example.com/
```

`server deploy` fails before writing any shared app's files if a listed network does not exist. compost never creates them: they belong to your compose projects.

**Undo:** `docker compose -p compost-ingress-caddy-main stop` and start the old proxy again.

Notes:
- Caddy requests new certificates for every domain. With many domains, mind [Let's Encrypt's rate limits](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/); move them in batches by adding sites over several deploys.
- Later changes to `sites` are reloaded without restarting Caddy. Changes to ports or `networks` restart it for a moment.

## Phase 2: shared services

Add compost's Postgres (and Keycloak, if you want logins) next to the old databases. They publish no ports and use their own networks, so nothing conflicts.

Register every old database that apps will keep using as an **external** database. compost does not run it, but apps can link to it and backups can dump it:

```yaml
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
    - name: shop-db                   # the old database container
      type: postgres
      version: 16                     # its major version
      external:
        host: db                      # service or container name on that network
        network: shop_default
```

```sh
compost server deploy --apply
compost server state
#   database   postgres18       postgres 18  running
#   database   shop-db          postgres 16  external, accepting connections
```

An external database is only used by links that name it with `instance`, so adding one never changes which database other apps get. A hosted database (AWS RDS and similar) is registered the same way, without `network` (see [External databases](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases)).

## Phase 3: apps, one by one

### Where compost.yaml lives

- **In the app's repository**, next to its compose file, if you can change it.
- **In a deployment repository** when the app is not yours, or you don't want compost files in it. `deployment.source_dir` points to a checkout of the app:

```
deploy/                         your repository
├── shop/
│   ├── compost.yaml            source_dir: ../upstream/shop
│   ├── compose.migrate.yaml    changes to the app's compose file
│   └── .compost-prod.yaml      domains, passwords (not committed)
└── upstream/shop/              the app's repository: a submodule or a checkout of a tag
```

`compost app generate --compose-file ../upstream/shop/docker-compose.yaml` in `deploy/shop/` writes a `compost.yaml` with `source_dir` set.

An app whose images are pulled (no `build`) needs only its compose file: `source_dir` can point to a folder that holds just that file.

### Write the configuration

The app links to its old database through the external database, with the credentials it already uses:

```yaml
# deploy/shop/compost.yaml
name: shop
deployment:
  source_dir: ../upstream/shop
  compose_overrides: [compose.migrate.yaml]
  build: true
services:
  database:
    - name: main
      type: postgres
      instance: shop-db              # the external database
      targets: [backend, migrate]
      environment:
        DATABASE_URL: db_url
  ingress:
    - name: site
      routes:
        - {name: api, target: backend, port: 5000}
app_services:
  - {name: backend, service: backend}
  - {name: migrate, service: migrate}
backup:
  volumes: [visits]
```

```yaml
# deploy/shop/.compost-prod.yaml
prefix: prod
services:
  database:
    - {name: main, db_name: shop, db_user: shop, db_password: the-current-password}
  ingress:
    - {name: site, domains: [shop.example.com, www.shop.example.com]}
```

compost passes the variables named in `environment` (here `DATABASE_URL`) to the services, built from the external database's host and these credentials. It adds the database's network to them too. Variables in the app's own compose file with the same name are overridden.

The app's compose file often also runs its database and a proxy, and the new deployment must not start them again. Its volumes must be the existing ones. `compose_overrides` changes that without editing the file:

```yaml
# deploy/shop/compose.migrate.yaml
services:
  db: {profiles: [legacy]}            # not started: the old container keeps running
  proxy: {profiles: [legacy]}
  migrate:
    depends_on: !reset {}             # it waited for `db`
volumes:
  visits:                             # the old deployment's volume, used as it is
    external: true
    name: shop_visits
```

`!reset` needs Docker Compose 2.24 or newer. Check what will happen:

```sh
compost app deploy --dry-run -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

### Test first (stateless apps only)

An app that keeps no data can run next to the old one under a temporary domain, e.g. `domains: [shop-new.example.com]`, until you are happy with it. **Don't do this with an app that writes to its database or volumes**: two copies would write the same data.

### Cut over

```sh
docker compose -p shop stop backend migrate   # the old app; its database keeps running
# remove the `shop` entry from `sites` in compost-server.yaml, then:
compost server deploy --apply                 # Caddy reloads, no restart
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
curl https://shop.example.com/api/health
```

While the site still serves the domain, `app deploy` refuses it: `domain shop.example.com is served by site shop`. The site goes first.

The downtime is the time the deploy takes, mostly building images when `build: true`. Images from a registry only need a pull.

**Undo:** `compost app remove shop-prod --yes`, put the site back, `compost server deploy --apply`, `docker compose -p shop start backend`. The old database and volumes were used in place, so they have everything.

From now on the app is a compost app: `compost app backup shop-prod` already saves its database (dumped from the external one) and its volumes.

## Phase 4: data into compost

When it suits you, move an app's data into compost's Postgres and compost-named volumes. It takes a short stop of that app, and uses only backup and restore:

```sh
compost app backup shop-prod -o shop-before-move.compost.tar.gz
```

Change the configuration:
- `compost.yaml`: remove `instance: shop-db`, so the link uses compost's Postgres (or pin `instance: postgres18`).
- `.compost-prod.yaml`: remove `db_password`, so compost generates one. Keep `db_name`/`db_user`, or remove them too for the defaults.
- `compose.migrate.yaml`: remove the external `visits` volume, so compost uses `shop-prod_visits`.

Then:

```sh
compost app deploy --no-apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml   # the new link; creates nothing yet
compost app restore shop-before-move.compost.tar.gz --include links,volumes --yes
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

`app restore` creates the database and user in compost's Postgres and loads the dump. It also copies the volume. The last deploy switches the app over and removes the link record of the old database. The old database itself is not touched, so you can compare or go back. Requests that reach the app between the restore and the last deploy still go to the old database, so stop the app's traffic for that minute if that matters.

The same procedure moves a database from or to a hosted one: point the link to another `instance`.

**Undo:** put the old configuration back and deploy it.

### Keycloak

compost does not move realms between Keycloak servers. Either:

- export each realm, with its users, from the old Keycloak as Keycloak documents it ([Importing and exporting realms](https://www.keycloak.org/server/importExport): `kc.sh export --realm shop --users realm_file`, run while that Keycloak is stopped). Import the file in compost's admin console (*Create realm* → *Resource file*). Then point the app's `oidc` link at it with `realm: shop`: compost adds its own client and the users it lists next to the imported ones, and leaves the rest of the realm alone.

- or let an `oidc` link create a fresh realm, its client and test users ([Applications](Applications.md#oidc-links)), when old accounts need not survive.

## Phase 5: clean up

When no site proxies to an old network any more, and no app links to an old database:

1. Remove the old networks from `networks` and the external databases from `compost-server.yaml`, then `compost server deploy --apply`. compost forgets an external database once no app links to it. Do this first: Docker won't remove a network while Caddy is still attached to it.
2. Remove the old projects once their data is safely in compost and backed up: `docker compose -p shop down`, then the old volumes (`docker volume rm shop_dbdata`, …).

## Checklist per app

- [ ] Domains, database credentials and volumes noted; backup taken
- [ ] `compost.yaml`, overlay and `compose.migrate.yaml` written; `--dry-run` shows the expected links
- [ ] Old app stopped, site removed, app deployed, domains checked
- [ ] `compost app backup` works
- [ ] Later: data moved into compost, overrides removed, old containers removed

---

<!-- Applications.md -->

# Applications

An app is a compose file plus `compost.yaml`, which says how compost links its services to the server's shared apps. Each deployment is an **instance** named `<app>-<prefix>`, e.g. `myapp-staging`. The full list of keys is in [Configuration](Configuration.md#compostyaml).

## Start from your compose file

```sh
cd myapp                       # has docker-compose.yaml
compost app generate [--compose-file compose.yaml] [--name myapp]
```

This writes `compost.yaml`, with one `app_services` entry per compose service and commented-out links, and `.compost.secrets.example.yaml` for the per-instance values. Neither needs a server.

A minimal `compost.yaml` for a web service behind the ingress, with a database:

```yaml
name: myapp
deployment:
  build: true                  # build images on the server (uploads the folder)
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      routes:
        - {name: api, target: backend, port: 5000, path: /api}
        - {name: web, target: web, port: 8080}           # path "/" by default
  database:
    - name: main-db
      type: postgres
      version: ">=16"
      targets: [backend]
      environment:
        DATABASE_URL: db_url
app_services:
  - {name: web, service: web}
  - {name: backend, service: backend}
```

And the overlay of one instance, `.compost-staging.yaml`:

```yaml
prefix: staging
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      domains: [staging.example.com]
```

## Services

`app_services` gives compose services the names that links use, and can add fixed variables:

```yaml
app_services:
  - name: backend
    service: backend-webapp    # the service in the compose file
    environment:
      APP_MODE: production
```

Compose services not listed are deployed as they are, but links can't target them. compost never changes your compose file: it writes an override file on the server that adds networks and variables.

## Sources in another folder

`compost.yaml` doesn't have to live in the app's repository. In a separate deployment repository, `source_dir` points to the app's folder: that folder is uploaded (with `build: true` or `attach_sources: true`) and holds the compose file.

```yaml
name: shop
deployment:
  source_dir: ../upstream/shop          # relative to compost.yaml
  compose_file: docker-compose.yaml     # relative to source_dir
  compose_overrides: [compose.prod.yaml]   # relative to compost.yaml
```

`compose_overrides` are compose files applied after the app's own, as with `docker compose -f … -f …`. With them you can change an app you can't or don't want to edit: turn off services (`profiles: [off]`), reuse existing volumes (`external: true` with `name:`), change images or resources. Relative paths inside them refer to `source_dir`. They are uploaded with the sources as `.compost/compose-override-<n>.yaml`, so backups and restores include them.

`compost app generate --compose-file ../upstream/shop/docker-compose.yaml` sets `source_dir` for you. See [Migration](Migration.md#where-compostyaml-lives) for a full layout.

## Ingress links

An ingress entry routes domains to services. Domains usually differ per instance, so they go in the overlay.

```yaml
services:
  ingress:
    - name: site
      optional: false          # true: skip this entry (with a notice) when no domains are given
      domains: [example.com, www.example.com]
      routes:
        - name: ui
          target: web          # an app_services name
          port: 8080           # the container port
          path: /ui            # default "/"
          strip_prefix: false  # true: /ui/x reaches the service as /x
```

Longer paths win, `/` comes last, and paths no route matches get a 404. A domain can be used by only one instance on a server.

A route can also serve another link of the app instead of a service, with `link: <kind>/<entry>`. This is how a Keycloak realm gets its own domain; see [OIDC links](#oidc-links).

## Database links

A database link creates a database and a user in a matching Postgres and passes the connection values to services:

```yaml
services:
  database:
    - name: main-db
      type: postgres
      version: ">=16"          # requirement on the major version; default "*"
      instance: postgres18     # optional: this shared app, when several match
      targets: [backend, migrate]
      environment:             # variable → link value
        DATABASE_URL: db_url
        PGHOST: db_host
```

| Link value | Example |
|---|---|
| `db_host` | `postgres18` |
| `db_port` | `5432` |
| `db_name` | `myapp_staging_main_db` |
| `db_user` | `myapp_staging_main_db` |
| `db_password` | generated on the first deploy, then kept |
| `db_url` | `postgres://user:password@postgres18:5432/dbname` |

In the overlay you can set `db_name`, `db_user` and `db_password`. The defaults come from `<app>_<prefix>_<entry>`, so renaming the entry gives a new, empty database unless you set them.

**Existing databases.** To link to a database compost doesn't run, register it as an [external database](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases) and pin it with `instance`. Unless compost has root credentials for it, give the existing `db_name`, `db_user` and `db_password`. compost then only passes them to the services:

```yaml
    - name: main
      type: postgres
      instance: shop-db
      db_name: shop
      db_user: shop
      db_password: …           # in the overlay
```

## OIDC links

An OIDC link creates a realm, a client and optionally users in a Keycloak, and passes the client settings to services:

```yaml
services:
  oidc:
    - name: login
      type: keycloak
      version: ">=26"
      realm: myapp                     # default <app>-<prefix>; created if missing
      client_id: web                   # default <app>-<prefix>-<entry>
      public_client: false             # true: no client secret, e.g. for a single-page app
      redirect_uris: ["https://staging.example.com/*"]   # required, usually in the overlay
      web_origins: []
      client_secret: …                 # secret; generated on the first deploy, then kept
      users:                           # secret; created if missing, passwords set on every deploy
        - {username: alice, email: alice@example.com, first_name: Alice, last_name: Doe, password: …}
      targets: [backend]
      environment:
        OIDC_ISSUER: oidc_issuer
        OIDC_CLIENT_ID: oidc_client_id
        OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET: oidc_client_secret
```

| Link value | Example |
|---|---|
| `oidc_issuer` | `https://auth.example.com/realms/myapp` |
| `oidc_internal_url` | `http://keycloak:8080/realms/myapp`, for server-to-server calls |
| `oidc_realm` | `myapp` |
| `oidc_client_id` | `web` |
| `oidc_client_secret` | empty for public clients |

**A realm on its own domain.** Add `public_url` to the link and an ingress route that serves it:

```yaml
services:
  oidc:
    - name: login
      public_url: https://login.example.com
  ingress:
    - name: login-page
      domains: [login.example.com]
      routes:
        - {name: realm, link: oidc/login}     # no target, port or path
```

That domain serves only `/realms/<realm>` and `/resources`; the admin console and other realms get a 404 there. The issuer and login pages use `public_url`. Links that share a realm must agree on it.

## Monitoring links

A monitoring link sends the output of services to a [monitoring app](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#openobserve-monitoring), has their Prometheus metrics scraped, and passes the collector's address to services that send OpenTelemetry data themselves:

```yaml
services:
  monitoring:
    - name: telemetry
      optional: true                   # skip (with a notice) when the server runs no monitoring app
      instance: monitoring             # optional: this shared app, when there are several
      targets: [web, backend]          # their output is collected; they get the variables
      logs: true                       # false: only variables and metrics
      metrics:                         # Prometheus endpoints, on any app service
        - {target: backend, port: 9100, path: /metrics}   # path "/metrics" by default
      environment:
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: otlp_endpoint
        OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: service_name
        OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: resource_attributes
```

| Link value | Example |
|---|---|
| `otlp_endpoint` | `http://monitoring:4318`, OTLP over HTTP |
| `otlp_grpc_endpoint` | `http://monitoring:4317` |
| `otlp_protocol` | `http/protobuf` |
| `service_name` | `backend`: the compose service of each target |
| `resource_attributes` | `service.namespace=myapp-staging,deployment.environment=staging` |

Services in `targets` and `metrics` join the monitoring network as `<instance>-<service>`. The collector picks up a metrics endpoint once the app runs, without a restart.

compost collects the output with Docker's `fluentd` log driver, set in its override file, so `docker logs` keeps working. A service that sets its own `logging` in the compose file can't be a target with `logs: true`: the deploy fails and says so.

## Deploying

```sh
compost app deploy [--apply | --no-apply] [-f files] [--prefix <prefix>] [--purge <kind>] [--dry-run]
```

`-f` defaults to `compost.yaml`. Add overlays with `-f compost.yaml,.compost-staging.yaml`. If the instance has an overlay stored on the server ([Secrets](Secrets.md)), it is merged right after the first file. `--prefix` overrides the prefix from the files (default `main`).

A deploy:

1. validates the config and checks the compose file's service names (exit 2 on errors);
2. checks the server and picks a shared app for each link (exit 3 if none matches, or a domain is taken);
3. uploads the sources: the whole folder with `build: true` or `attach_sources: true`, otherwise only the compose file. Left out: `.git/`, files given with `-f`, `.compost-*.yaml`, `.compost.*.yaml` and patterns in `.compostignore` (gitignore syntax);
4. writes the override file and link records. **Without `--apply` it stops here.**
5. with `--apply`: creates databases, users and realms; runs `docker compose build` (with `build: true`) or `pull`; then `up -d --remove-orphans`; waits up to 60 s until every service runs (or is healthy) or has exited with code 0; removes dropped links; updates Caddy's routes.

The result is shown as by `app state`. Running the same deploy again keeps data and passwords and doesn't recreate unchanged containers.

**Dropped links.** When a link of the last deploy is no longer in the config (removed, renamed, an optional ingress without domains, or now matching another shared app), the deploy removes it after the new containers run: its record, routing and scraping go, its data stays (collected logs and metrics stay in the monitoring app). Add `--purge database` (or `oidc`) to delete that data too. `--dry-run` lists them first.

## Inspecting

```sh
compost app list                                 # every instance: status, running, last update
compost app state myapp-staging                  # or: -f compost.yaml,.compost-staging.yaml / --app myapp --prefix staging
```

`app state` shows the instance's status, each compose service (running, exited, health), domains and routes, and databases (never passwords). It exits 4 if something is not healthy. A service that exited with code 0, like a migration, counts as healthy, unless it has `restart: always` or `unless-stopped`.

Both read what the deploy stored on the server, so they don't need the app's repository.

## Removing

```sh
compost app remove myapp-staging [--volumes] [--purge database,oidc] [--yes]
```

Removes the routes and link records, then `docker compose down` and the instance's folder. Databases and realms stay unless their kind is in `--purge` (databases on an external server stay anyway, see [External databases](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases)); `--volumes` also removes the compose volumes, except external ones. It asks for confirmation unless `--yes`. A stored overlay ([Secrets](Secrets.md)) stays, so deploying the instance again brings it back as it was.

## Validation errors

Errors name the place in the config, e.g. `services.ingress[site].routes[api]: target "backnd" is not in app_services`. Exit code 2 means the files are wrong (nothing was changed), 3 means the server didn't allow it (no matching shared app, a domain used by another instance).

---

<!-- Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md -->

# Servers and shared apps

## Defining servers

```sh
compost server define prod --address 203.0.113.10 [--user compostuser] [--port 22] [--identity-file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519] [--server-home <path>]
compost server define dev --local          # this machine, no SSH
compost server define prod --address 198.51.100.7 --force   # replace; keeps the server's settings
compost server list
compost connect prod                       # default server for following commands
compost disconnect
```

Defining a server only writes `~/.compost/servers.yaml` (see [Configuration](Configuration.md#serversyaml)). compost's folder on the server, `--server-home`, defaults to `~/.compost-server`.

Every command that talks to a server uses, in order: `-s/--server <name>`, the `COMPOST_SERVER` environment variable, the context from `connect`. With none of them set it fails with exit code 2.

### Connections

compost runs POSIX `sh` scripts on the server through a single `ssh` call each, and streams files as tar. It shares one SSH connection per run and keeps it open 60 s for the next command (`ControlMaster`, sockets in `~/.compost/ssh/`). It uses your SSH config, agent and host key checking as they are.

Add `-v` to any command to print every script it runs on the server.

## Server state

```sh
compost server state
```

| Status | Meaning | Exit code |
|---|---|---|
| `OK` | compost manages the server and every shared app runs (and is healthy, if it has a healthcheck) | 0 |
| `UNINITIALIZED` | Reachable, nothing deployed by compost yet | 0 |
| `DEGRADED` | Some shared app is not running | 4 |
| `UNREACHABLE` | The SSH connection fails | 3 |
| `NO_DOCKER` | `docker` or `docker compose` doesn't work for the server user | 3 |
| `FOREIGN` | Another manager key manages this server (see [Installation](Installation.md#set-up)) | 3 |

Commands that change a server run these checks first, and stop on `UNREACHABLE`, `NO_DOCKER` and `FOREIGN`.

## Deploying shared apps

```sh
compost server generate [--with caddy,postgres,keycloak,openobserve] [--force]
compost server deploy [--apply | --no-apply] [-f files] [--dry-run]
```

`server generate` writes starter files to the current folder (`compost-server.yaml`, `compost-server.prod.yaml`, `.compost-server.secrets.example.yaml`; see [Production setup](Production-Setup.md#3-shared-apps)). It adds types that a chosen type needs: `keycloak` brings `postgres` and `caddy`, `openobserve` brings `caddy`. `--list` shows the available types.

`server deploy` reads `compost-server.yaml` and `.compost-server.secrets.yaml` from the current folder, or the files given with `-f`. It:

1. validates the config (exit 2 on errors, before anything touches the server);
2. creates compost's folder and the Docker networks;
3. renders each shared app's files and uploads them, generating missing passwords;
4. with `--apply`: starts every shared app with `docker compose up -d` and waits until it runs, then prints `server state`. A shared app starts after the shared apps it needs running (Keycloak after its database and Caddy); links to a monitoring app don't count, so Caddy can send its logs to the OpenObserve it serves.

Without `--apply`, only steps 1–3 run. `--dry-run` shows what would happen and changes nothing. Running it again changes nothing that didn't change: unchanged containers are not recreated. When only Caddy's sites changed, Caddy reloads them without a restart.

When a shared app loses a link (say its `monitoring` is removed), the deploy with `--apply` removes the link and recreates the shared app without it.

Shared apps removed from the config are reported as `orphaned` and keep running; stop them with `docker compose -p compost-<kind>-<name> down`.

## Shared app types

A server has at most one ingress, and any number of databases, OIDC providers and monitoring apps. Every shared app has a `name` (lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 31 characters, starting with a letter), a `type`, a `version` and optionally an `image`. Type-specific settings go in `configuration`.

### caddy (`ingress`)

Reverse proxy for every app's domains, with automatic HTTPS.

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      version: 2
      configuration:
        http_port: 80
        https_port: 443
        tls: auto
        acme_email: admin@example.com
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `2` | Only `2` |
| `image` | `caddy:<version>-alpine` | |
| `configuration.http_port` | `80` | Host port |
| `configuration.https_port` | `443` | Host port, TCP and UDP |
| `configuration.tls` | `auto` | How sites get certificates: `auto`, `internal` or `off`, see [TLS](#tls) |
| `configuration.acme_email` | – | Contact for the ACME account. Only with `tls: auto` |
| `configuration.networks` | `[]` | Existing Docker networks Caddy joins too, so `sites` can reach containers compost doesn't manage. Never created: `server deploy` fails if one is missing |
| `configuration.sites[]` | `[]` | Sites written by hand: `name`, `domains`, and `config`, the inside of a Caddyfile site block |
| `configuration.access_log` | `false` | Log every request, as JSON, to Caddy's output. With [`monitoring`](#monitoring-shared-apps), the log goes to OpenObserve. An app's site gets it on the app's next `app deploy` |

```yaml
      configuration:
        networks: [shop_default]
        sites:
          - name: shop
            domains: [shop.example.com]
            config: |
              reverse_proxy backend:5000
```

`sites` are for services compost doesn't deploy, typically while [migrating](Migration.md). A domain belongs to a site or to an app, not both: `app deploy` refuses a domain a site serves, and `server deploy` refuses a site for a domain an app serves.

#### TLS

`configuration.tls` applies to every domain Caddy serves, apps' and `sites` alike:

| Value | Certificates | Ports |
|---|---|---|
| `auto` | From Let's Encrypt, renewed by Caddy. Every domain needs public DNS pointing to the server and port 80 or 443 reachable from the internet before the first deploy. HTTP redirects to HTTPS | `http_port` and `https_port` |
| `internal` | Signed by Caddy's own local CA. Browsers warn unless they trust its root certificate, `data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt` in the Caddy folder. For test servers and domains without public DNS | `http_port` and `https_port` |
| `off` | None: sites are served over plain HTTP. For a local machine, or behind another proxy that terminates TLS | `http_port` only; `https_port` is not published |

`acme_email` is the contact Let's Encrypt uses for expiry warnings; compost refuses the config when it is set with any `tls` other than `auto`. Certificates are kept in `data/` (see [Files and folders](Files-and-Folders.md)) and are part of `server backup`, so a restored server doesn't request them again.

With [`monitoring`](#monitoring-shared-apps), Caddy also serves its Prometheus metrics (requests, durations, sizes per host) on port 9180 inside its container, not published on the host, and the collector scrapes them. This needs Caddy 2.8 or newer; the default image is.

Caddy runs as the server user, so its files can be backed up and removed without root. Hosts and paths no app uses get a 404. When an app is deployed, Caddy is reloaded, not restarted; a site that fails `caddy validate` is rolled back and fails the deploy.

### postgres (`database`)

A Postgres server. Each app link gets its own database and user.

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
      image: postgres:18-alpine
      configuration:
        root_password: …    # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | required | Major version, matched against apps' `version` requirements |
| `image` | `postgres:<version>` | An official `postgres` image or a compatible one |
| `configuration.root_password` | generated | Superuser password. Secret. Can't change after the first deploy |

Postgres is not published on a host port. Only containers on its network `compost-db-<name>` reach it, at host name `<name>`, port 5432.

### keycloak (`oidc`)

An OpenID Connect provider for app logins. It needs a `postgres` database with version 18 or newer and the ingress, both on the same server: compost creates its database `compost_oidc_<name>_db` and routes the domain of `url` to it.

```yaml
shared:
  oidc:
    - name: keycloak
      type: keycloak
      version: 26
      configuration:
        url: https://auth.example.com
        admin_password: …   # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `26` | Major version |
| `image` | `quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.6` for 26 | Required for other versions |
| `configuration.url` | required | Public URL, `https://<domain>` or `http://<domain>[:port]`, no path |
| `configuration.admin_user` | `admin` | Administrator in realm `master` |
| `configuration.admin_password` | generated | Secret. Only used on the first start; can't change later |
| `configuration.database.instance` | – | The database to use, when several match |

Its data lives in that database: back them up and restore them together. Apps reach it on network `compost-oidc-<name>` at `http://<name>:8080`. Keycloak gets 180 s to start. See [Applications](Applications.md#oidc-links) for linking apps to it.

### openobserve (`monitoring`)

Collects logs, metrics and traces of apps and shared apps, and shows them in [OpenObserve](https://openobserve.ai)'s UI. It runs two containers:
- **openobserve** stores the data in `shared/monitoring/<name>/data/` and serves the UI. Only the collector and the ingress reach it.
- **collector**, an [OpenTelemetry Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/), receives what apps send and forwards it to OpenObserve. Apps reach it on network `compost-monitoring-<name>` at host name `<name>`, without credentials; only the collector knows OpenObserve's password.

```yaml
shared:
  monitoring:
    - name: monitoring
      type: openobserve
      version: 1
      configuration:
        url: https://logs.example.com
        retention_days: 30
        root_password: …    # in .compost-server.secrets.yaml
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` | Major version |
| `image` | `openobserve/openobserve:vX.Y.Z` for 1 | Required for other versions |
| `configuration.url` | – | Public URL of the UI, `https://<domain>` or `http://<domain>[:port]`, no path. compost routes its domain through the ingress. Without it, the UI is not reachable |
| `configuration.root_email` | `admin@compost.local` | Login of the root user. Can't change after the first deploy |
| `configuration.root_password` | generated | Secret. 8 or more characters with a lowercase and an uppercase letter, a digit and a special character, as OpenObserve requires. Can't change after the first deploy |
| `configuration.retention_days` | OpenObserve's (10 years) | Days data is kept |
| `configuration.forward_port` | `24224` | Port on the server's `127.0.0.1` where Docker delivers the output of linked containers. Each monitoring app needs its own |
| `configuration.container_metrics` | `true` | CPU, memory, network and disk I/O of every container on the server. The collector reads them from the Docker socket, mounted read-only; that gives the collector control over Docker, like root on the server. `false` leaves the socket out |
| `configuration.collector_image` | `otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:X.Y.Z` | |

What ends up in OpenObserve (organization `default`):
- **Logs** stream `docker`: the output of linked containers, with `fluent_tag` (`<instance>.<service>`, e.g. `myapp-prod.backend` or `compost-ingress-caddy-main.caddy`), `container_name`, `source` (`stdout`/`stderr`) and the Compose project and service.
- **Logs** stream `default`, **traces** and **metrics** that apps send with OpenTelemetry (OTLP).
- **Metrics** scraped from the Prometheus endpoints of links, labeled `compost_app`, `compost_prefix` and `compost_service`, and the `container_*` metrics.

Log in with `root_email` and `root_password`; compost writes both to `connectors/monitoring/<name>/root-connector.yaml` on the server. Apps link to it with [`services.monitoring`](Applications.md#monitoring-links).

The log driver sends asynchronously: linked containers start and run while the collector is down, and `docker logs` keeps working.

## Monitoring shared apps

`monitoring` on a shared app sends its output, and the metrics it serves, to a monitoring app:

```yaml
shared:
  ingress:
    - name: caddy-main
      type: caddy
      configuration:
        access_log: true
      monitoring: {}
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      type: postgres
      version: 18
      monitoring: {metrics: false}
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `monitoring.instance` | – | The monitoring app to use, when there are several |
| `monitoring.logs` | `true` | Collect the output of its containers |
| `monitoring.metrics` | `true` | Scrape its metrics, if it serves any: Caddy does |

Caddy, Postgres and Keycloak can be monitored. External shared apps and monitoring apps can't. It works in both directions: OpenObserve's domain is served by the Caddy that sends its logs to it. On the first deploy, Caddy starts before OpenObserve, and Docker keeps Caddy's output in a small buffer and sends it once the collector runs.

## External databases

A database compost doesn't run (an existing Postgres container, or a hosted one such as AWS RDS) can be added with `external`. Apps then link to it like to any database, and `app backup` dumps it.

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: shop-db                    # an existing container on this server
      type: postgres
      version: 16                      # its major version
      external:
        host: db                       # service or container name
        network: shop_default          # existing network to reach it on
    - name: rds-main                   # AWS RDS
      type: postgres
      version: 16
      external:
        host: main.abc123.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com
        sslmode: require
      configuration:                   # optional; root_password in the secrets file
        root_user: postgres
        root_password: …
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `external.host` | required | Host name or address, as the app's containers see it |
| `external.port` | `5432` | |
| `external.network` | – | Existing Docker network the database is on; linked services join it. Without it, containers reach the host like any other address |
| `external.sslmode` | – | `disable`, `allow`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca` or `verify-full`; added to `db_url` and used by compost's own clients |
| `external.allow_purge` | `false` | Let `--purge database` drop databases there (needs root credentials) |
| `configuration.root_user` | `postgres` | Superuser, if compost may create databases there |
| `configuration.root_password` | – | Its password; secret |

What compost does with it:
- **Runs nothing.** `server deploy` only checks that `network` exists and stores how to reach it. `server state` checks that it answers (`external, accepting connections`); if it doesn't, the state is `DEGRADED`.
- **Links pin it.** A link uses an external database only with `instance: <name>`, so adding one never changes which database other apps get.
- **Without root credentials**, links name an existing database, user and password (`db_name`, `db_user`, `db_password`), and compost creates nothing. **With them**, compost creates databases and users as on its own Postgres.
- **Backups** run `pg_dump` and `psql` in a temporary `postgres:<version>-alpine` container on the server. The credentials go into an env file readable only by the server user, deleted after the run, never onto a command line. `server backup` leaves external databases out: `app backup` saves the apps' databases.
- **Never destroys data by accident.** `--purge database` keeps databases there, with a warning, unless root credentials are set and `allow_purge: true`.
- Removed from `compost-server.yaml` while no app links to it, it is forgotten by the next `server deploy`.

Database names and users must be lowercase letters, digits and `_` (as compost's own); rename others before linking.

## Inspecting links

```sh
compost connector list
```

```
database
└─ postgres18  postgres 18  running
   ├─ myapp-prod/main-db  database myapp_prod_main_db, user myapp_prod_main_db  app: deployed
   └─ myapp-staging/main-db  database myapp_staging_main_db, user myapp_staging_main_db  app: deployed
ingress
└─ caddy-main  caddy 2  running
   ├─ myapp-prod/site  example.com  / → myapp-prod-web:8080  app: deployed
   └─ myapp-staging/site  staging.example.com  / → myapp-staging-web:8080  app: deployed
```

Links of shared apps (Keycloak's database and domain) show as `shared <kind>/<name>/<entry>`. A link whose instance no longer exists shows as a leftover record.

## Locks

Commands that change a server hold a lock (`~/.compost-server/lock/`), so two can't run at once. If a command was killed and left it behind, the next one prints who held it; add `--force-unlock` to remove it.

---

<!-- Secrets.md -->

# Secrets

Passwords and other per-instance values (domains, database credentials, OIDC users) live in **overlays**: YAML files merged over `compost.yaml`. You can keep an overlay on your machine and pass it with `-f`, or store it on the server with `compost secret deploy`.

## Rules

- Commit only examples: `.compost.secrets.example.yaml`, `.compost-staging.example.yaml`. compost never loads `*.example.yaml` by itself.
- Keep the real files out of Git, e.g. with `.compost-*.yaml` and `.compost.*.yaml` in `.gitignore`, keeping the examples with `!*.example.yaml`.
- Files named `.compost-*.yaml` or `.compost.*.yaml`, and every file passed with `-f`, are never uploaded with the sources.
- Passwords you leave out are generated on the first deploy (32 hexadecimal characters; OpenObserve's root password starts with `Compost-` to meet its rules), stored on the server and reused by later deploys.
- On the server, secret files have mode `0600`. Secrets never appear in output, `--dry-run` (shown as `***`), stored configs or remote command lines.

## Local overlays

```sh
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-staging.yaml
```

Simple, but every machine that deploys needs the file.

## Overlays stored on the server

```sh
compost secret deploy .compost-staging.yaml [--prefix staging]
compost app deploy --apply --prefix staging      # compost.yaml + the stored overlay
compost secret list
compost secret remove --app myapp --prefix staging
```

The stored overlay must name its app (`name: myapp`). The prefix is `--prefix`, else the file's `prefix`, else `main`. It is kept at `~/.compost-server/secrets/apps/<app>/<prefix>.yaml`.

`app deploy` merges it right after the first file: `compost.yaml` → stored overlay → other `-f` files. Local overlays can still override stored values.

- `secret deploy` replaces the stored overlay as a whole. If the new one leaves out a link that only the old one defined (say an ingress entry with its domains), the next `app deploy` drops that link. Run `app deploy --dry-run` first to see the effect.
- `app remove` keeps the stored overlay, so deploying the instance again restores it as it was. `secret remove` deletes it.
- `app backup` saves it in the archive and `app restore` puts it back; such an archive then holds secrets.

## Shared apps

Secrets of shared apps go in `.compost-server.secrets.yaml`, next to `compost-server.yaml`, which `server deploy` loads by default:

```yaml
shared:
  database:
    - name: postgres18
      configuration:
        root_password: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
  oidc:
    - name: keycloak
      configuration:
        admin_password: change-me-to-a-long-random-string
  monitoring:
    - name: monitoring
      configuration:
        root_password: Change-me-to-a-long-random-string-1
```

Lists merge by `name`, so only the secret keys are repeated. The passwords are optional, and none can change after the first deploy. Generated ones are on the server:

```sh
cat ~/.compost-server/shared/database/postgres18/secrets/postgres.env
grep PASSWORD ~/.compost-server/shared/oidc/keycloak/secrets/keycloak.env
grep root_ ~/.compost-server/connectors/monitoring/monitoring/root-connector.yaml
```

## Notes

- Every instance linked to the same shared app is on that shared app's Docker network. Networks don't isolate instances from each other yet.
- Apps send data to a monitoring app's collector without credentials: any container on its network can. Only the collector holds OpenObserve's password.
- Server backups hold root passwords and link credentials. Keep archives as safe as the server.

---

<!-- Backup-and-Restore.md -->

# Backup and restore

```sh
compost app backup myapp-prod                       # links, sources, volumes → myapp-prod-<time>.compost.tar.gz
compost app backup --all                            # every instance in one archive
compost app backup myapp-prod --link main-db --format raw   # just the SQL dump
compost app restore myapp-prod-….compost.tar.gz --prefix review -f review.yaml   # a copy of the app
compost server backup                               # shared apps: data, config, secrets
compost server restore prod-….compost.tar.gz          # onto a new server, then `app restore`
compost backup list                                 # archives on the server
```

Backups take the server's lock, so they never run during a deploy.

## Targets

Where archives go: `--target` for backups, `--source` for restores. The default is `backup.target` in `compost-server.yaml`, else `local`.

| Target | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `local` | Streamed through the SSH connection to this machine and packed here. Nothing stays on the server. `-o` is a file or folder here. |
| `server` | Packed on the server in its backup folder (`backup.server_path`, default `~/.compost-server/backups`). No data crosses the network. `-o` and restore archives are file names in that folder, or absolute paths. |
| `s3` | Not implemented yet (exit 2). |

```yaml
# compost-server.yaml
backup:
  target: server
  server_path: backups      # absolute, or relative to compost's folder on the server
```

## Formats

| `--format` | Writes | Restorable |
|---|---|---|
| `compost` (default) | `<name>.compost.tar.gz` with a manifest and the configuration needed to restore | yes |
| `raw` | Only the data: one item as a plain file (e.g. a `.sql` dump), several as `<name>.tar.gz` | no |

Archives get mode `0600` and never overwrite an existing file. Default names: `<app>-<prefix>-<UTC yyyymmdd-hhmmss>`, `apps-<time>` for `--all`, `<server>-<time>` or `<server>-<shared app>-<time>`.

## App backup

```sh
compost app backup [<instance> | -f files | --app <name> --prefix <prefix> | --all]
                   [--include links,sources,volumes,images] [--link <entry>]… [--stop]
```

| Part | Saved |
|---|---|
| `links` | Database dumps (`pg_dump`, plain SQL); ingress and monitoring records and site files, for reference. Collected logs and metrics are not part of an app backup |
| `sources` | The uploaded sources (only the compose file when the folder isn't uploaded) |
| `volumes` | The named volumes listed under `backup.volumes` in `compost.yaml` |
| `images` | `docker save` of the services' images |

The default is `links,sources,volumes`. The stored config is always saved, and the overlay stored with `secret deploy`, if any. `--link main-db` or `--link database:main-db` saves only that link.

Volumes must be listed to be saved:

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [uploads]       # top-level `volumes:` keys of the compose file
```

Links to an [external database](Servers-and-Shared-Apps.md#external-databases) are dumped too, from a temporary `postgres` client container on the server, with the link's own credentials.

For a consistent copy of files that a service keeps writing, stop it while the volumes are copied. `backup.stop` names those services (`true` for all); `--stop` stops all of them for one backup. They start again afterwards, as do the services that Compose stopped with them; services that weren't running stay stopped.

```yaml
backup:
  volumes: [uploads, search-index]
  stop: [worker, indexer]
```

## Steps around a backup or restore

Some data must be prepared before it is copied, e.g. a database that runs inside the app is dumped into a volume, and loaded from it after a restore. Steps run commands in the instance's services:

```yaml
# compose file
services:
  db:
    image: mariadb:11
    environment: {MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: …}
    volumes: [db-dumps:/dumps, db-data:/var/lib/mysql]
  backup-job:                     # started only by the step: the profile keeps `app deploy` from starting it
    image: myorg/backup-tools
    profiles: [backup]
    volumes: [uploads:/uploads]
volumes: {db-dumps: {}, db-data: {}, uploads: {}}
```

```yaml
# compost.yaml
backup:
  volumes: [db-dumps, uploads]
  before_backup:
    - exec: db
      command: mariadb-dump -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --all-databases --single-transaction > /dumps/all.sql
    - run: backup-job             # its own command; or `command: [prepare, --fast]`
  after_backup:
    - {exec: db, command: rm -f /dumps/all.sql}
  after_restore:
    - {exec: db, command: mariadb -uroot -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" < /dumps/all.sql}
```

| Step | Runs | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `exec: <service>` | `docker compose exec` in the running container; needs `command` | the service isn't running, or the command exits with an error |
| `run: <service>` | `docker compose run --rm`: a new container, removed afterwards; `command` replaces the service's own | the command exits with an error |

A string `command` runs with `sh -c` in the container, so `>`, `<`, `&&` and the container's variables work; a list (`[mariadb, --version]`) runs as is. Steps run on the server in order and their output is shown. They come from the config stored by the last `app deploy`, so deploy after changing them.

| List | When |
|---|---|
| `before_backup` | Before anything of the instance is saved, while its services run. A failed step stops the backup. |
| `after_backup` | After the data is saved and the stopped services started again. Also runs when the backup or a `before_backup` step failed, to clean up; its own failures are warnings. |
| `before_restore` | When data is loaded into a deployed instance (restore without sources): before its services are stopped. A failed step stops the restore. Not run by a restore with sources: that instance only starts after its data is loaded. |
| `after_restore` | After the data is loaded and the services are ready (healthy, for services with a healthcheck), in both kinds of restore. A failed step fails the restore. |

The backup steps run when the backup saves links or volumes (not for `--include sources` or `images` alone).

## App restore

```sh
compost app restore <archive> [--instance <instance> | --all] [--prefix <prefix>] [-f overlays]
                    [--include …] [--link …]… [--replace] [--yes]
```

**With sources** (the default when the archive has them), it deploys the instance from the archive as `app deploy --apply` would, then loads databases, images and volumes before the services start. The archived config is the base; `-f` overlays are merged over it and `--prefix` changes the instance. That makes copies:

```sh
compost app restore myapp-prod-20261015-120000.compost.tar.gz --prefix review -f review-domains.yaml
```

The copy needs other domains (one domain, one instance), and its databases follow the new prefix unless the config sets `db_name`.

**Without sources** (`--include links,volumes`), it loads data into the deployed instance: it lists what will be replaced, asks unless `--yes`, stops the services, loads, and starts them again.

Both run the instance's [restore steps](#steps-around-a-backup-or-restore): those of the restored config with sources, those of the deployed instance without.

Databases and volumes that already hold data are only replaced with `--replace` (exit 3 otherwise). A link's database is created first if it doesn't exist yet, e.g. after `app deploy --no-apply` of a link that moved to another database.

## Moving an app's data to another database

Back up, point the link at the other database, render the deploy without starting it, load the data, deploy:

```sh
compost app backup myapp-prod -o before.compost.tar.gz
# compost.yaml: change `instance` of the database link (e.g. from an external database to compost's)
compost app deploy --no-apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
compost app restore before.compost.tar.gz --include links,volumes --yes
compost app deploy --apply -f compost.yaml,.compost-prod.yaml
```

The old database is left as it was. Volumes move the same way when their name changes, e.g. after removing an `external` volume from a compose override. See [Migration](Migration.md#phase-4-data-into-compost).

## Server backup and restore

```sh
compost server backup [--shared <name>]… [--format …] [-o …] [--target …]
compost server restore <archive> [--shared <name>]… [--source …] [--yes]
```

A server backup holds the stored `compost-server.yaml`, all link records and each shared app's data: Postgres `pg_dumpall` and its password file; Caddy's certificates, config and `sites`; OpenObserve's data folder and root login.
